title: “BE WATCHFUL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK—AND ONE DAY, YOU MAY WISH YOU HAD UNDERSTOOD IT SOONER
paragraphs: “BE WATCHFUL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK—AND ONE DAY, YOU MAY WISH YOU HAD UNDERSTOOD IT SOONER

Jesus was not teaching His followers to live terrified of tomorrow. He was warning them about something far more dangerous: a heart that can slowly fall asleep while the body is still sitting in church.
There is a frightening kind of sleep that has nothing to do with closing your eyes.
You can wake up every morning.
Even sit beneath preaching every Sunday...
Not because you stopped believing God exists.
Not necessarily because you openly rejected Jesus.
But because somewhere between yesterday’s conviction and today’s distractions, eternity stopped feeling urgent.
Repentance became something other people needed.
The Bible became familiar enough to quote but not powerful enough to interrupt you.
And Jesus became Someone you believed in without necessarily being Someone you were actively watching for.
That is why some of Christ’s most unsettling words were not spoken only to atheists, pagans, or people openly hostile to God.
They were spoken to people who were supposed to be waiting for Him.
“Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.”
That little word “watch” can sound harmless in English.
Like standing beside a window and looking into the distance.
But the language behind the New Testament gives the warning sharper teeth.
The Greek verb used in Matthew 24:42 is γρηγορεῖτε — grēgoreite, from γρηγορέω — grēgoreō.
Its sense is to stay awake, to remain alert, to maintain vigilance.
Jesus was not telling His disciples to stare nervously at the sky.
And suddenly this becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps the greatest danger in your Christian life is not always the scandal everyone can see.
Sometimes it is the sleep nobody notices.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
But something inside you has grown numb.
There was once a time when certain sins broke your heart.
There was once a time when missing prayer bothered you.
Now weeks can become months of hurried sentences thrown toward heaven.
There was once a time when Scripture confronted you.
Now you mostly search for verses that comfort you.
There was once a time when you wondered,
Now the first question is often,
One ignored conviction at a time.
One secret habit at a time.
One resentment you refuse to surrender.
One apology you refuse to make.
Perhaps no word has carried more unfinished repentance than tomorrow.
Jesus understood something about the human heart that we desperately need to recover.
We assume spiritual catastrophe will always announce itself dramatically.
But sometimes destruction begins with drowsiness.
That is why, in Gethsemane, only hours before the crucifixion, Jesus gave His disciples another warning.
Peter, James, and John were exhausted.
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.”
The suffering of Christ was approaching.
“What, could ye not watch with me one hour?”
Then came the warning generations of believers desperately need:
“Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσεύχεσθε — grēgoreite kai proseuchesthe.
Not so that you can impress God with your spirituality.
Not so that you can become paranoid about demons hiding behind every inconvenience.
Not so that Christians spend their lives trying to decode every headline into an end-times timetable.
Peter believed he was stronger than he actually was.
Earlier he had effectively insisted that even if others stumbled, he would remain faithful.
He slept when Jesus told him to watch.
Soon afterward, when pressure arrived, Peter denied knowing Christ.
That is terrifying because Peter's failure did not begin beside the charcoal fire where he denied Jesus.
Something was already happening before that moment.
And perhaps somebody reading this recognizes the pattern.
You keep thinking your greatest danger is the moment temptation arrives.
But often the battle has already been influenced by what happened before temptation arrived.
The message you should never have answered.
The website you told yourself you would visit only once.
The relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
The pride nobody was permitted to confront.
The Bible gathering dust while your screen receives hours of your attention.
and suddenly you discover how weak you really are.
Jesus did not say the flesh might be weak.
That means spiritual watchfulness begins with humility.
A pastor is not beyond temptation.
A worship leader is not beyond temptation.
A theologian is not beyond temptation.
A Christian who has followed Jesus for fifty years is not beyond temptation.
The moment we begin believing, “I would never do that,” we may already be standing somewhere dangerous.
“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.”
The Greek behind “be vigilant” again uses the language of wakefulness:
Peter had learned this lesson painfully.
The man who once slept when Jesus told him to watch would later tell suffering Christians:
That changes how those words feel.
Peter was not writing as someone who had never failed.
He was writing as someone who knew what failure tasted like.
He knew what it was like to make a courageous promise...
He knew what it was like to insist on his loyalty...
He knew what it was like to hear the rooster.
He knew what it was like to realize Jesus had been right about him.
Maybe you know something about bitter tears.
Maybe your rooster has already crowed.
Maybe your marriage carries scars from something you did.
Maybe pornography has been hiding behind your screen.
Maybe alcohol became the place you run when life hurts.
Maybe nobody knows how angry you really are.
Maybe jealousy has poisoned relationships you once treasured.
Maybe you have been pretending spiritually for so long that you are terrified to admit how far your heart feels from God.
Maybe you once burned for Jesus.
Now you barely recognize the person you have become.
And perhaps the most painful sentence inside you is:
Yet Peter's story did not end with a rooster.
And yours does not have to end with your worst night either.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere moral improvement.
If the Gospel were simply “watch harder, behave better, never fail,” Peter's story would be hopeless.
But Jesus went to the cross.
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree...”
Peter understood grace because Peter needed grace.
And after the resurrection, Jesus did something astonishing.
John 21 records a scene beside another charcoal fire.
The man who denied Jesus beside a fire now sat before the resurrected Jesus beside a fire.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Not because Peter could erase what happened.
But because failure would no longer be permitted to have the final word over his life.
Not that sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
Jesus called people to repent and believe the Gospel.
But your scandal does not have greater authority than Christ's grace.
Your failure does not have greater authority than Christ's blood.
Your darkest chapter does not get to steal the pen from the resurrected King.
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
That does not mean Jesus merely helps us feel better about remaining unchanged.
Biblical grace is not permission to sleep.
“Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.”
“See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time...”
And there are things you cannot recover once they are gone.
You cannot return to yesterday and pray the prayer you refused to pray.
You cannot return to your children's childhood after they have grown.
You cannot reclaim every conversation you wasted.
You cannot guarantee yourself another opportunity to apologize.
You cannot promise yourself another year.
“Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh.”
Being watchful, then, is not date-setting.
Jesus explicitly said His followers do not know the hour.
Watchfulness means living today in such a way that Christ's appearing would not expose a life deliberately built around spiritual sleep.
Testing what you hear against Scripture.
Remembering that Satan is real but Christ is greater.
Remembering that your flesh is weak but God's grace is sufficient.
Remembering that this world is temporary.
And remembering that watchfulness is not ultimately staring anxiously into darkness.
It is remaining faithful to Jesus while waiting for the dawn.
Paul gives us one of Scripture's most beautiful summaries:
“Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity.”
Then everything is wrapped in love.
Biblical watchfulness does not turn Christians into suspicious, angry people obsessed with finding darkness everywhere.
A truly watchful believer should become increasingly anchored in truth and increasingly shaped by love.
Humble enough to recognize your own weakness.
Tender enough to notice somebody else suffering.
Loving enough not to weaponize it.
Wise enough to run from it.
Secure enough in Christ to rise again.
And awake enough to realize there are people around you who may be spiritually dying while appearing perfectly fine.
Perhaps that is why you needed to read this today.
But perhaps you are not the only one.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list whose smile is hiding a war.
Someone who believes Jesus could never want them after what they have done.
Someone spiritually sleeping who does not realize how far they have drifted.
Send this privately to someone who has been drifting.
And if something in this exposed a place you have been hiding, do not perform for anybody.
Someone reading the comments may discover that Christians are not people who never bleed.
We are people whose wounds keep leading us back to Christ.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, and salvation is God's gift—not something we purchase or earn.

But Scripture also teaches believers to participate willingly and generously in Gospel work. Paul spoke appreciatively of believers who partnered with him in the Gospel, and Christian generosity is meant to flow from grace rather than coercion.

So if you genuinely want another practical way to glorify God, consider helping Gospel-centered truth travel farther. Pray. Share Scripture. Encourage someone who is struggling. Support faithful Gospel work where God gives you conviction and ability.
And support is not only financial.
Sharing can reach the person money never could.
But after all of that, remember this:
The purpose is not Gospel Warrior.
A shared Facebook post cannot save you.
Just you standing honestly before God.
Has something been slowly replacing Jesus at the center of your life?
Is there a sin you keep renaming because calling it sin would require repentance?
Is there somebody you need to forgive?
A relationship you need to surrender?
A secret you need to bring into the light?
Have you confused knowing about Christ with actually following Him?
Not because Christ wants you terrified.
Because He loves you too much to let you comfortably sleep through a war for your soul.
And the same Jesus who met Peter after his failure still receives repentant sinners.
The cross proves your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
The empty tomb proves grace is more powerful than you dared to hope.
And when you fall, do not run farther into darkness.
Because one day the watching will end.
The King we have waited for will no longer seem distant.
And help somebody else stay awake too.
Your worst chapter may explain your tears—but it does not get to write your ending when the scarred hands of Jesus are still holding the pen.
